title: State Sharing Between Hooks
description: Explore strategies for sharing state between custom hooks using refs, contexts, and external stores.

data.text: Welcome to this comprehensive guide on **State Sharing Between Hooks**. Explore strategies for sharing state between custom hooks using refs, contexts, and external stores. By the end of this lesson, you will have a thorough understanding of State Sharing Between Hooks and be confident in applying it to your projects.
Sharing State with Refs

Refs are the simplest mechanism for sharing mutable state between hooks. Because refs persist across renders without triggering re-renders, they are ideal for synchronizing values that hooks read but do not display directly.

data.title: Shared State via useRef
data.content: Two hooks sharing a counter without re-rendering on every change.

data.title: Refs vs State
data.text: Use refs when you need to share mutable data without causing re-renders. Use state when changes should trigger a re-render. In most UI scenarios, you will use both together.
Dependency Injection with Context
Context allows you to inject shared state into hooks without prop drilling. This is especially useful when a hook needs access to configuration or a store that lives higher in the tree.

data.title: Theme Hook via Context
data.content: Injecting theme configuration into custom hooks using React Context.

data.text: External Store Pattern

React 18 introduced the `useSyncExternalStore` hook for subscribing to external data sources. This pattern is perfect for sharing state between hooks when you want to avoid context re-render overhead.

data.content: A lightweight reactive store shared between multiple hooks.

data.text: When to Use Each

data.title: Decision Guide
items: Use refs when sharing mutable data that does not need to trigger renders
Use context when multiple components at different levels need the same state
Use external stores when you need concurrent-safe subscriptions or want to share state outside React
Combine patterns: context can provide a store instance, and hooks use useSyncExternalStore to subscribe

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Refs share mutable state without re-rendering
Context injects shared state through the component tree
External stores provide concurrent-safe subscriptions via useSyncExternalStore
Choose the lightest pattern that satisfies your re-rendering requirements
data.takeaway: State sharing between hooks is about choosing the right balance between simplicity and reactivity.

data.text: Common Mistakes to Avoid

Even experienced developers can fall into these traps when working with **State Sharing Between Hooks**. Being aware of these common mistakes will help you write better code and avoid costly debugging sessions:

items: **Over-Engineering**: Using advanced features of State Sharing Between Hooks when a simple solution suffices. Always start with the simplest approach that meets your requirements and add complexity only when justified.
**Ignoring Edge Cases**: Failing to handle null values, empty states, and boundary conditions leads to runtime errors and poor user experience.
**Copy-Paste Without Understanding**: Using code snippets without fully understanding their implications creates hidden bugs and security vulnerabilities.
**Neglecting Testing**: Assuming code works without tests is a recipe for production incidents. Write tests that verify behavior and prevent regressions.
**Performance Blindness**: Ignoring performance implications until they become critical issues. Profile early and optimize based on data, not assumptions.
**Hardcoding Configuration**: Embedding values directly in code instead of using environment variables and configuration files.
**Tight Coupling**: Creating dependencies that make code difficult to test, modify, or reuse. Favor composition over inheritance.
**Inconsistent Error Handling**: Mixing different error handling patterns makes code unpredictable and hard to debug.

data.text: Performance Considerations

Performance is a critical aspect of any production application. When implementing **State Sharing Between Hooks**, consider these optimization strategies to ensure your application remains fast and responsive:

items: **Lazy Loading**: Defer non-critical operations until they are actually needed to reduce initial load time.
**Caching**: Implement intelligent caching strategies to avoid redundant computations and network requests.
**Memoization**: Cache results of expensive function calls to improve performance for repeated operations.
**Batch Processing**: Group multiple operations together to reduce overhead and improve throughput.
**Resource Management**: Properly clean up resources, event listeners, and subscriptions to prevent memory leaks.
**Profiling**: Use performance profiling tools to identify bottlenecks before optimizing.
**Bundle Size**: Minimize dependencies and use tree-shaking to reduce application bundle size.
**Network Optimization**: Reduce payload sizes, use compression, and implement efficient data fetching strategies.

data.text: Security Considerations
Security should never be an afterthought. When implementing **State Sharing Between Hooks**, keep these security best practices in mind to protect your application and users:

items: **Input Validation**: Always validate and sanitize user input to prevent injection attacks.
**Authentication and Authorization**: Implement proper access controls and verify user permissions.
**Secrets Management**: Never hardcode API keys, passwords, or tokens. Use environment variables and secret management services.
**HTTPS**: Always use HTTPS in production to encrypt data in transit.
**Content Security Policy**: Implement CSP headers to mitigate XSS attacks.
**Dependency Scanning**: Regularly scan dependencies for known vulnerabilities.
**Rate Limiting**: Protect APIs from abuse with appropriate rate limiting.
**Audit Logging**: Log security-relevant events for monitoring and incident response.
